title.narrative: NIGER-NIGERIA REPORT OF THE YEAR 2 NARRATIVE FINAL REPORT ON STRENGTHENING CROSS-BORDER COOPERATION IN COMBATING TRAFFICKING IN PERSONS

description.narrative: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY The Niger-Nigeria Anti-Trafficking Project has successfully completed its 24 months of initial implementation and three (3) months of two (2) consecutive no-cost extensions, aiming to reinforce bilateral relations between the two countries with a focus on combating human trafficking. Headed by the Joint Technical Working Group (JTWG), the project sought to operationalize the provisions of the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed by both countries through a detailed annual work plan. This plan addressed critical areas such as prevention, investigation, prosecution, and protection of victims of trafficking, thereby contributing to the dismantling of trafficking and smuggling networks. The overarching goals of the project were to: - Strengthen bilateral cooperation between Niger and Nigeria. - Improve coordination and efficiency in combating human trafficking. - Enhance victim assistance mechanisms. - Contribute to the dismantling of trafficking and smuggling networks. Key Achievements - Joint Research: ANLTP and NAPTIP conducted a first-of-its-kind Trafficking in Persons (TiP) prevalence study in the border regions of Niger and Nigeria, providing valuable data for analysis and future actions. - Joint Standard Operating Procedures (JSOPs): Established joint guidelines, or a Bilateral Referral Mechanism (BRM), aimed at standardizing the protection and assistance given to trafficked persons across both countries. - Frontline Responders Directory: Developed a consolidated list of frontline responders to expedite action in human trafficking cases. - Strengthened Prosecution and Investigation: Enhanced cooperation between respective TiP agencies, ANLTP in Niger and NAPTIP in Nigeria, especially in the areas of investigation and prosecution. - MoU signed between Niger and Nigeria: The agreement serves as an innovative framework for combatting human trafficking by reinforcing bilateral cooperation and coordination between the two nations. The MoU is the first operationalized agreement of its kind in West Africa.1 - Improved Communication: Built robust communication channels between ANLTP and NAPTIP, enabling real-time consultation and collaboration. Impact - Victim Return: Reports indicate a systematic increase in bilateral coordination leading to the successful return of trafficking victims since the signing of the MoU and the establishment of the JTWG as a cooperation and coordination framework. - Enhanced Anti-Trafficking Capabilities: The initiation of targeted training programs has substantially elevated the skill sets of law enforcement agencies in both countries. This capacity building equips them for effective joint actions against human trafficking. - Sub-Committee’s Autonomy and Preparedness: Sub-committees within the JTWG have shown a high degree of independence and initiative, effectively planning, and preparing for joint operations. These sub-committees are now well-positioned to continue the implementation of their activities in the project's second phase to solidify their capacity, in a sustainable manner. 1 Similar agreements have been signed in Mali, Cote d’Ivoire, Benin, and Gambia. In 2023, UNODC commenced the implementation of the provisions of the agreement signed between Nigeria and Gambia in a project funded by the Netherlands (Dutch MFA). Niger – Nigeria Annual Report 2022-2023 NL-ICMPD DSH No. 4000004262 Page 3 of 17 Significance - The signing of an MoU is a pioneering effort, serving as a template for cooperation between two countries in the fight against human trafficking in the West Africa region. - Leadership from the Directors General of both NAPTIP and ANLTP and the growing professional and personal links among JTWG members indicate a firm foundation for continued collaborative work and trust-building. Future Directions - Intensify joint activities of the sub-committees. - Expand the training scope to include more law enforcement personnels. - Utilize findings from the joint research to inform future interventions. - Share project accomplishments with other national institutions across the region. The project has laid a strong foundation and serves as a model for combatting human trafficking through bilateral cooperation, showing promising signs of sustainable success. This report comes at the end of project implementation and offers a detailed review of the activities and outcomes. It highlights the advancements made since the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was signed, identifies challenges encountered and the steps taken to mitigate them, and outlines prospects for future phases and sustainability strategies. It serves as a crucial instrument for informing donors and other stakeholders about the project's overall achievements. Niger – Nigeria Annual Report 2022-2023 NL-ICMPD DSH No. 4000004262 Page 4 of 17 CONTEXT Niger serves as a central point for many West African migrants aiming for Europe, with Nigeria contributing the largest number of people transiting through the country. Often, these migrants are returned to Niger while attempting to cross the Sahara Desert en route to Libya, Algeria, and ultimately Europe. Consequently, Niger faces the daunting task of providing for these vulnerable individuals, many of whom are susceptible to ongoing vulnerability or even re-trafficking. Stranded migrants frequently reside in transit cities like Agadez, Arlit, and Dirkou, awaiting an opportunity to continue their journey. The Agadez region exemplifies the issues associated with migrant living conditions in areas already lacking basic amenities. The added population strain and the absence of feasible options for these in-transit migrants create tensions with local communities. The absence of a formal cooperative structure between Niger and Nigeria has generally led Niger to rely on international and humanitarian organizations to manage these intricate migration patterns. While Nigeria has endeavored to establish cooperative agreements with other ECOWAS members, the effectiveness of such agreements is often questioned due to inadequate structural support for their key objectives. To address this issue, the Joint Technical Working Group (JTWG) and its sub-committees were established under the Niger-Nigeria Trafficking in Persons (TiP) cooperation project. Their role is to facilitate actual implementation and serve as a blueprint for similar efforts in West Africa. For the initiative against human trafficking between Niger and Nigeria to be sustainable, stakeholders must go beyond dependence on international organizations. The JTWG's Partnership and Resource Mobilization sub-committee has conducted meetings to develop collaborative tools and roadmaps, seeking to involve both governmental and private sectors in resource mobilization for joint TiP actions. Effective coordination is necessary to ensure that the objectives of the JTWG are met in both countries and that the benefits of the existing framework are solidified. PROJECT IMPLEMENTATION Project Activities 1.1 Niger-Nigeria JTWG, Subcommittees and Secretariat Completed Year 1 1.1.1 Conduct and validate an assessment of SOM & TIP between NR & NG  1.2.1 JTWG Office in Niamey (ANLTP)  1.3.1 Develop Terms of Reference (ToR) for JTWG  1.3.2 Inauguration of JTWG & establishment of sub-committees  1.3.3 Elaborate JTWG annual workplan and implementation framework  1.3.4 Organized four (04) meetings per year of the JTWG  1.3.5 Organized monthly meetings of the sub-committees for JTWG workplan  Year 2 1.3.6 Implement sub-committees’ activities in line with JTWG workplan  1.3.6.1 Investigation and Prosecution Sub-Committee  1.3.6.2 Victim Protection and Assistance  1.3.6.3 Sensitization on TiP at least 2 events/yr)  1.4.1 Organized annual regional conference on TIP Lessons Learnt  2.1 Strengthen Capacities of Actors in NG & NR Completed 2.1.1 Develop joint SOPs for transnational referral of victims  Niger – Nigeria Annual Report 2022-2023 NL-ICMPD DSH No. 4000004262 Page 5 of 17 2.1.2 Development of a directory of first line responders  2.2.1 Train first line responders on the victim-centered approach  2.2.2 Organized joint capacity building trainings for JTWG  2.3.1 Develop and produce sensitization tools/materials   Completed Activity • Activity 1.3.3 JTWG Workplan - Year 2 The work plan for joint activities was finalized during the JTWG's fourth meeting, which took place in Niamey, Niger, in February 2022. The following collaborative actions were slated for implementation: - Approval of the following four sub-committees responsible for executing the JTWG actions: 1) Prevention 2) Protection and Repatriation 3) Investigation and Prosecution 4) Partnership and Resource Mobilization - Coordinated training for border law enforcement units. - Collaborative instruction sessions for staff from NAPTIP (Nigeria's agency against trafficking) and ANLTP (Niger's counterpart). - Combined training for staff at shelters to better understand each agency's operational methods. - Collective efforts to provide support and medical services to victims. - A joint study to assess the extent of Trafficking in Persons (TiP) in border regions between Niger and Nigeria. - Strengthening the administrative capabilities of both involved agencies. - A three-way agreement among Niger, Nigeria, and the International Centre for Migration Policy Development (ICMPD) to formalize the initiative. - Specialized training opportunities for JTWG members focusing on TiP issues. - Establishing a communication platform for intelligence sharing between ANLTP and NAPTIP. - Setting up shelter facilities in both Agadez and Niamey in Niger. These measures aim to bolster the collaborative efforts between Niger and Nigeria in addressing human trafficking and related issues, building upon the existing framework for more effective results. • Activity 1.3.4 Organize 4 JTWG Meetings/yr In conjunction with the ECOWAS’ Annual Review Meeting of national TiP focal points, the project organized the fourth meeting of the JTWG in Niamey on 03-04 February 2022 at the Noom Hotel Niamey and had 30 persons in attendance drawn from various government agencies, international organizations, and civil society organizations. The ANLTP Director General Ousmane Mamane and the NAPTIP Director General Prof. Fatima Waziri-Azi co-chaired the fourth meeting of the JTWG. The ANLTP Director General delivered the opening speech as host country, while NAPTIP Director Niger – Nigeria Annual Report 2022-2023 NL-ICMPD DSH No. 4000004262 Page 6 of 17 General gave her goodwill messages. The Goodwill message from the Netherland was delivered through a pre-recorded video by Ms. Mylene Sijnja. The highlight of the 4th JTWG was the participation of JTWG members in the 14th Annual Review Meeting (ARM) of the ECOWAS Regional Network of National Focal Institutions Against Trafficking in Persons Plus (RNNI-TIP+) and the showcasing of the Niger-Nigeria cooperation model. The operationalization mechanism of the MoU raised a lot of interest among the other participants of the ARM. The fifth meeting of the JTWG held in Lagos on 24-27 May 2023 at Radisson Blu Hotel Ikeja with 42 persons in attendance and 6 members of the Dutch MFA delegation. The ICMPD Head of West Africa Region, Ag. DG of ANLTP-TIP DG, Head of the Administration and Training Department, Ag. DG of NAPTIP, Director of Research and Development gave their introductory remarks. Ms. Mylene Sijnja, Migration Policy Officer, MFA delivered a goodwill message on behalf of the Dutch delegation. The overall outcome of the 5th JTWG meeting focused more on the need for sub-committees to carry out planned joint activities in both countries and at the end, hold a final JTWG to assess the impact of project activities. Also, the project organized the sixth meeting of the JTWG/Final Evaluation in Niamey on 06-07 March 2023 at Noom Hotel Niamey and had 41 persons in attendance. The ICMPD Director of Migration Dialogues and Cooperation, the Head of West Africa Region, Ag. DG of ANLTP-TIP DG, Head of the Administration and Training Department, Ag. DG of NAPTIP, and Director of Research and Development gave their introductory remarks. Senior Policy Officer at the Embassy of the Netherlands, Mr. Seydou Amadou, delivered a goodwill message on behalf of the Dutch MFA. The sixth session offered an opportunity for NAPTIP, ANLTP, and partner agencies in Niger, especially CSOs to take stock of project achievements and opportunities to discuss openly project successes and challenges. • Activity 1.3.6.1 Investigation and Prosecution The Subcommittee on Investigation and Prosecution is tasked with overseeing the coordination of investigations into human trafficking and migrant smuggling, as well as the ensuing legal proceedings. Initial discussions revolved around the current state of intelligence sharing and law enforcement collaboration between the two nations. Both sides stressed the importance of enhancing thorough investigations, including the application of specialized investigative approaches and effective intelligence utilization. Though Niger and Nigeria engage in routine police meetings under the formal framework established by the 2003 Accra Agreements on criminal policing, most on-the-ground interactions occur through informal channels like phone calls, WhatsApp, and emails. This is largely driven by the urgency often required in investigations. Formalized communication does occur through systems like I-24/7 and the Consular General in Kano when necessary. During the fifth JTWG meeting, the subcommittee explored ways to deepen cooperation and fulfill the wider objectives set forth in the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) for more effective case investigation and prosecution. Key areas of focus in improving communication included: - Establishing a trusting environment that enables unhindered intelligence sharing without jeopardizing ongoing investigations. - Conducting bilingual training to overcome language barriers. - Simplifying procedural complexities. Niger – Nigeria Annual Report 2022-2023 NL-ICMPD DSH No. 4000004262 Page 7 of 17 In-depth dialogues revealed the unique capacities of each country and highlighted considerable opportunities for effective collaboration. This is particularly evident in the planning of undercover operations. Since the MoU was signed, DST Niger has transferred 80 victims and facilitated the conviction of 12 suspects in the Nigerian states of Kano and Jigawa. Members of the subcommittee observed that specific trafficking routes, such as those crossing Babura and Tinkim in Jigawa and Zinder States, have seen improved security due to coordinated efforts. Additionally, around 80 convictions were reported in 2022 for transnational cases involving both nations. • Activity 1.3.6.2 Victim Protection and Assistance Following the signing of the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between Niger and Nigeria, the project helped to shift focus from relying solely on international organizations for coordinating the actions between two national institutions, the project facilitated direct government-to-government coordination in the identification and repatriation of human trafficking victims. Within the framework of the Subcommittee on Protection and Repatriation, specific actions were designed to address the immediate needs of victims in shelters in both countries. These joint initiatives centered on: 1. Organizing training programs to build expertise of caregivers in addressing victims’ needs, trauma counseling, and shelter management, as well as establishing a bilateral referral system for victims. 2. Providing health-focused outreach programs for victims of human trafficking. 3. Distributing welcome kits, which include hygiene items, to victims upon their arrival at the shelters. During the healthcare outreach programs, medical volunteers offered specialized consultations in several areas: - Family Medicine - Obstetrics & Gynecology - Optometry - Psychiatry - Dentistry Victims received comprehensive and high-quality medical evaluation from a carefully selected team of professionals, followed by testing, diagnosis, and provision of necessary treatment. The distribution of welcome kits aimed to restore the self-esteem of the victims and foster a sense of belonging, thereby facilitating more effective reintegration and rehabilitation efforts. Overall, the project directly aided in the protection and assistance of over 1,200 vulnerable migrants, comprising 60% children (primarily girls and boys) and 40% adults (majority women). Nigeria Niger Location Number of Victims Supported Location Number of Victims Supported Abuja 80 Zinder 370 Benin 150 Agadez 200 Lagos 160 Kano 100 Katsina 80 Enugu 60 Niger – Nigeria Annual Report 2022-2023 NL-ICMPD DSH No. 4000004262 Page 8 of 17 Total 630 Total 570 Overall, NAPTIP has recorded that over 800 VoTs have been transferred from Niger to Nigeria, including children. Since the signing of the MoU between Niger and Nigeria, the project notes that there has been increased government to government collaboration in the return of victims of trafficking. Considering the success and impact of the outreach initiative, NAPTIP in her sustainability plan has included medical outreach to all shelters as part of her mandate, hence a stronger synergy and collaboration with the Nigeria Medical Association was established to provide adequate medical assistance to the victims in all the shelters, at least twice a year. Niger on the other hand is also committed to establishing such collaboration with key stakeholders in the country to improve the overall condition of VoTs. Along these communities, circa 20,000 persons were reached by the awareness raising campaigns and targeted distribution of flyers, T-shirts, and others sensitization tools . As recorded in the previous year, the major output of the two sensitization activities carried out by NAPTIP and ANLTP within the framework of the Niger Nigeria project created community awareness and education along the border corridor on trafficking trends and the modus operandi of traffickers as part of proactive preventive measures to reduce the risk of vulnerable members of the community in Niger and Nigeria. The target audiences were reached with over 50,000 combined sensitization materials shared amongst community members to create awareness of TiP/SoM. Targeted communities were sensitized, and commitments were secured from various heads/groups to join the fight against TiP. Border officials, traditional institutions, and community leaders including the youths and religious institutions joined the sensitization campaign. Against the backdrop of these sensitization activities in both Niger and Nigeria, there is a unanimous plea by the community leaders requesting both NAPTIP and ANLTP/TIM to have frequent sensitization activities along the border corridor to heighten the level of awareness and to significantly reduce the menace of human trafficking. Some of the recommendations for future programs suggested by the community leaders included: 1. Establishment of community advocacy groups in the border areas 2. Training of the advocates for integration as informants 3. Training of Law enforcement officers in the border areas 4. Expansion of team to include secretariats and advance party team. 5. Deployment of monitoring and evaluation mechanisms 6. Sustainability and target group expansion Niger – Nigeria Annual Report 2022-2023 NL-ICMPD DSH No. 4000004262 Page 10 of 17 Figure 8&9 : Dialogue, TiP Caravan Activities in Niger Republic Figure 10 : TiP Sensitization Activities to Market Women, Transporters and Youths in Niger Republic Niger – Nigeria Annual Report 2022-2023 NL-ICMPD DSH No. 4000004262 Page 11 of 17 Figure 11: Dialogue, Really and Caravan Activities in Nigeria Niger – Nigeria Annual Report 2022-2023 NL-ICMPD DSH No. 4000004262 Page 12 of 17 Figure 12-17: TiP Sensitization; Sports, Inter-University Debates, Military School Vanguards Activities in Nigeria • Activity 1.4.1 Annual Regional Conference on TiP Lessons Learnt The ECOWAS Commission in close collaboration with the ICMPD organized the 2021/14th Edition of the Annual Review Meeting of the ECOWAS Regional Network of National Focal Institutions against Trafficking in Persons Plus (RNNI-TIP+) from 01-03 February 2022 in Niamey, Niger. Amongst the specific objectives of the ARM was to conduct on spot assessment of the level of implementation of the ECOWAS Plan of Action to Combat Trafficking in Persons (2018-2022). During the technical sessions, the Director General of both NAPTIP and ANLTP made presentations to showcase Niger-Nigeria Cooperation on TiP project. The bilateral framework and milestones was presented to the ECOWAS members states. • Activity 2.1.1 Joint SOPs for Transnational Referral of Victims The major output of the protection and repatriation subcommittee meeting in Lagos on 24-26 May 2022, comprising of stakeholders from both countries birthed the joint standard operating procedures (JSOPs) also referred to the Bilateral Referral Mechanism and the Directory of First Line Responders. The committee dedicated these three days to study the national referral mechanism of both countries with the guidance of a consultant, teased out relevant framework and produced a working document. The final draft of both documents was presented at the JTWG meeting chaired by the DGs of the leading agencies, preceding the subcommittee meetings to critique the document. After thorough evaluation and the plenary on the fourth day, the document was validated. Part of the recommendations from the JTWG include: • Need for the tracking of the victims using the common referral tools. • Training of shelter operators at both ends on how to identify, treat victims and protection needs. • Training of operational or managerial level stakeholders on the harmonized JSOP. • Joint workshops on the operationalization of the BRM. • Publication and dissemination of the BRM in both countries. • Presentation of bilateral referral mechanism to stakeholders. Niger – Nigeria Annual Report 2022-2023 NL-ICMPD DSH No. 4000004262 Page 13 of 17 • Activity 2.1.2 Development of a Directory of First Line Responders As highlighted in activity 2.1.1, the major output of the protection and repatriation subcommittee meeting in Lagos on 24-26 May 2022, comprising of stakeholders from both countries birthed the joint directory of first line responders. Part of the recommendations from the JTWG include: • Capacity building of first line responders and their roles in identification, care, reception, rehabilitation, and reintegration of victims • Need for the tracking of the victims using the common referral tools • Periodic stakeholders mapping and update of the directory, at least yearly • Training of operational or managerial level stakeholders on the harmonized directory • Provision of common database • Activity 2.2.1 Train First Line Responders on the Victim-Centre Approach Following the subcommittee meetings and 5th JTWG meeting in Lagos on 27 May 2022, one of the key priority activities for the protection and repatriation subcommittee centered on capacity building of first line responders in Niger and Nigeria. On Nigeria side, a total of 150 shelter operator and service providers are trained across three states where NAPTIP shelter are located – Abuja, Benin, Lagos. A total of 290 VoTs received medical assistance and welcome packs in November 2023 across Abuja, Benin, Lagos. Also, a total of 340 VoTs received medical support and welcome packs in June 2023 across Kano, Katsina, Enugu, and Lagos. Similarly, in Niger, the project provided training for 50 shelter operators, and 170 VoTs received medical support in January 2023 in Zinder. In addition, a total of 200 VoTs received medical support in both Zinder and Agadez respectively in June 2023. Amongst training provided to strengthen capacity of leading agencies and stakeholders include: • Capacity Building on tactical planning session for joint sting operation in reinforcing bilateral cooperation in Lagos. Niger – Nigeria Annual Report 2022-2023 NL-ICMPD DSH No. 4000004262 Page 14 of 17 • Role of NAPTIP and ANLTP care givers/shelter operators in protecting human rights of VoTs in Lagos, Nigeria and Zinder/Dosso, Niger respectively • Joint research study on prevalence of TiP in border areas of Niger and Nigeria The study on prevalence of TiP in border areas was conducted simultaneously by the two agencies on both sides of the border in June 2023. The same methodological approach was proposed to the two agencies to compare the data collected from corresponding mirror communities on both sides of the border. Two main methods were proposed for data collection, namely desk review and the interview/questionnaire survey. The desk review was to focus on data obtained from periodic qualitative and quantitative evaluations conducted by NAPTIP in Nigeria and the Ministry of Women's Promotion and civil society organizations in Niger. Structured questionnaires and interview guides were prepared to conduct surveys and on the field. Survey questionnaires were structured according to the following elements of analytical framework: i. Effectiveness of anti-TIP activities (gaps and bottlenecks) ii. Ownership of anti-TIP activities at border community level iii. Sustainability (anchoring at state and border community levels; cross-border collaboration with Niger) • Activity 2.3.1 Develop and Produce Sensitization Tool/Materials The major output of the two sensitization activities carried out by NAPTIP and ANLTP within the framework of the Niger Nigeria project created community awareness and education along the border corridor on trafficking trends and the modus operandi of traffickers as part of proactive preventive measures to reduce the risk of vulnerable members of the community in Niger and Nigeria. The target audiences were reached with over 50,000 combined sensitization materials shared amongst community members to create awareness of TiP/SoM. Targeted communities were sensitized, and commitments were secured from various heads/groups to join the fight against TiP. Border officials, traditional institutions, and community leaders including the youths and religious institutions joined the sensitization campaign. The project put together a narrative video documentary of the activities and achievement jointly implemented by both countries as communication tools. Training of the advocates for integration as informants Niger – Nigeria Annual Report 2022-2023 NL-ICMPD DSH No. 4000004262 Page 15 of 17 IMPLEMENTATION CHALLENGES • Building Trust The Niger-Nigeria project has successfully navigated the inherent challenges that come with establishing a novel form of cooperation in the West Africa region. While building trust and confidence between agencies within a single government can be difficult, doing so between agencies from different countries presents even more complexities. However, NAPTIP and ANLTP have been working diligently to reach the necessary level of confidence for the Joint Technical Working Group (JTWG) to be fully operational. The project has effectively fostered an atmosphere of mutual respect, equity, and fairness, treating both agencies as equal partners. The cooperation is steadily evolving, with mutual trust incrementally solidifying. In this way, the Niger-Nigeria project has been instrumental in facilitating this critical process of building inter-agency trust and collaboration. • JTWG Gender Disparity ICMPD has been proactive in addressing the challenges associated with achieving gender balance in the Joint Technical Working Group (JTWG), which is comprised of members from multiple departments and agencies (MDAs) from both Niger and Nigeria. Given that men make up a disproportionate percentage of public service in both countries—69% in Nigeria and 84% in Niger—it is understandable that the composition of the JTWG reflects this imbalance. To rectify this, ICMPD is committed to enhancing the representation of women from both nations within the group. Two more members were added from both sides making 4 additional members, all which are women. Through these efforts, ICMPD has helped to foster a more inclusive and equitable working environment that aligns with our core value of gender equality. • COVID-19 Travel Regulations The start of the project was severely impacted by the Covid-19 pandemic and general security situation in the Sahel, particularly in Niger. The implementation of such a project requires notably the ability to travel, and the year 2021 has been very problematic in this regard. Nevertheless, great strides were made in catching up with project activities and with two consecutive no-cost extensions of 3 months each, all planned activities and several new ones were implemented. • High Turnover of Leadership It is worth noting that a significant challenge encountered by the project was the extended vacancy of the Director-General position at NAPTIP throughout much of 2021. This role saw two brief appointments before finally being definitively filled in late October 2021, just days before the MoU between ANLTP-TIM and NAPTIP was signed. The lack of stable leadership made it challenging to secure formal direction and commitment, leading to a period of relative stagnation within the NAPTIP agency. The project also experienced a change in the Director-General of ANLTP. Although this transition was less disruptive compared to the situation at NAPTIP, a change in leadership inevitably requires time for the new Director to evaluate the merits and anticipated outcomes of an ongoing project for the agency. ICMPD was able to overcome this impediment by working through the heads of departments and the acting DG of NAPTIP. Niger – Nigeria Annual Report 2022-2023 NL-ICMPD DSH No. 4000004262 Page 16 of 17 • Security Situation in Niger Another complicating factor for the project commencement has been the security situation. Following Niger's presidential election in March 2021, an attempted rebellion was narrowly averted. Understandably, this event shifted the Nigerien Government's focus and priorities, creating an atmosphere of uncertainty that temporarily clouded the project's launch. However, after the initial slow start, the project eventually picked up pace. • Institutional Differences It is crucial to recognize the differences in the organizational structures and responsibilities of NAPTIP and ANLTP. NAPTIP is a larger agency, employing over 1,000 staff members and overseeing a comprehensive range of tasks in the fight against human trafficking, from investigation and prosecution to protection, repatriation, and reintegration. In contrast, ANLTP has a much smaller team of 20 personnel and serves as a coordinating body without any law enforcement functions. In Niger, law enforcement duties related to human trafficking are managed by the Border Police Force (DST), the Ministry of Interior, and the Ministry of Justice. The physical infrastructure of the two agencies is also quite different. NAPTIP has expansive headquarters and operates state and regional offices throughout Nigeria, while ANLTP's office in Niamey is considerably smaller and contends with a challenging work environment. However, this project is contributing to improvements; for instance, ANLTP will soon have an internet connection and other upgraded facilities. PROJECT OPPORTUNITIES The Memorandum of Understanding between Niger and Nigeria is a pioneering agreement in West Africa, serving as a gateway for further collaborative efforts. This MoU now lays the groundwork for official initiatives between two countries aimed at combating human trafficking. To capitalize on the Niger-Nigeria project and cement the gains already made, the following actions are necessary: - Intensify joint activities of the four (4) sub-committees. - Expand the project training scope to include more law enforcement personnel. - Utilize findings from the joint research to inform future interventions. - Share project accomplishments with other national institutions across the region.
